solo.name: Origin historian (WHY HELM)
solo.summary_plain: Helm is the learning part of the CNCM "pointer machine". It was built because the machine before it failed in a measured way. That older machine learned the questions it practised (84 to 86 of 189 right after training), but it did not improve on worlds it had never practised (5, 3 and 2 of 45). A check that cost nothing and used no model showed why: every world was blended into one input, so the old machine could not tell a new world apart. On 2026-09-19 the owner chose "option 1": a machine that reads one world as a small graph and answers by pointing at that world's own parts. The owner's standing rule, in his words, was "IT MUST BE LEARNING LEARNING AT THE NEURON LEVEL". The name "Helm" first appears in commit 994950b5 (2026-09-19 23:52 -0700). The changelog says only "The owner chose the name." I found no recorded reason for the name. For Helm 0.1, 1.0 and 2.0, "pass" meant one thing: a fixed grading program printed LEARNS_NEW_WORLDS on all three seeds (seeds are separate training runs that start from different random numbers). The lineage file misstates how Helm 2.0 failed that gate. Only seed 20260919 failed under the fixed grader, not two seeds. A second checker uses a stricter rule, so the records hold two definitions of "pass". Today's Q4 smoke run had no accuracy target set in advance, so 0 of 16 is a measured negative result, not a failed gate. The Q4 model is a separate lab model (a small GRU network, a basic kind of sequence network, with 70,818 learned numbers). It is not Helm in the lineage sense. The records say Helm 3.0 does not exist yet.

findings.claim: Helm exists to fix one measured failure of the machine that came before it (the typed practice study). That machine learned the worlds it practised and nothing about worlds it had never practised. A zero-cost measurement traced the cause to the input: it could not read a new world by construction. The owner then ordered a pointer machine, and the learning part of that pointer machine is what was named Helm.

solo.name: Design critic (WHY HELM: design rationale)
solo.summary_plain: Helm is the learning part of the CNCM pointer machine. The owner wanted learning that happens inside the network itself (CAS Native Cognitive Machine = CNCM). Helm's inputs were built with no words because the earlier machine could not read worlds it had never seen. That choice was sound. But it left inputs that a short fixed program (no learning) can answer exactly. Helm's reasoning loop (the repeated rounds) barely matters. Saved tests reset it to its starting weights and turned message passing off. Helm 1.0 and Helm 2.0 then lost at most 7 of 127 held-back answers, and one seed gained 4. Helm 2.0's big win, correspondence 20 of 20, is matched exactly by a rule that reads no links. The rule pairs parts in the order their names were declared. The analogy scorer never sees the world it is asked to compare against, so analogy cannot be learned as the scorer is built. In the Helm 3.0 lab, every task (families G, A, C) is solved exactly by an existing parser, lookup or sum. So a learned version can only copy those programs and carry them to new tree shapes. Today's Q4 smoke had 128 one-example updates. Its loss stayed above that of a counting rule that ignores the input. So 0/16 with one repeated tree says nothing yet about what R1 can learn. The path to the owner's goal breaks at two points. No planned task yet needs anything beyond the project's own fixed programs. And the Helm that the plan would plug CAS into has no working reasoning core that anyone has shown.

findings.claim: Helm's recurrent reasoning core (the ^6 block and its 8 shared rounds) does not carry the measured answers, in Helm 1.0 or in Helm 2.0. The runs' own post-run ablations reset each component to its initial weights on the 127 held-back questions. Resetting the core block changed the held-back score by 0, -3, 0 (Helm 2.0) and by -4, -2, 0 (Helm 1.0). Resetting the round group (node_encode, state_encode, round_mix, round_rate) resets round_rate to 0. Since tanh(0)=0, this switches message passing off completely. It changed the score by -3, -6, +4 (2.0) and -7, -2, -2 (1.0). Resetting the heads cost -55, -69, -73 (2.0). The design reason: each round's update is scaled by PER_ROUND_UPDATE_CAP 0.01 x tanh(round_rate), and round_rate starts at 0. The heads also get direct side inputs that answer one-hop questions without the loop: the a->b adjacency bit, each node's own degree one-hots, and degree sums. The F1 repair made multi-hop possible but did not make the loop matter. On the ten-node development panel, which needs long chains, Helm 2.0 p00->p10 went 3->2, 10->12 and 0->6 of 59. Helm 1.0 went 0->7, 0->9 and 0->6. The audit's diagnosis that the one-hop loop was the ceiling is therefore not supported as the binding limit. Directive D07 had warned about exactly this.

findings.claim: Is there a coherent path from these designs to the owner's goal? Only in part. The goal on record is learning 'AT THE NEURON LEVEL' toward a working CASFORMER/CNCM, and rule-layer gains never count. The directive's own discipline fits that goal: mechanism-free baselines, splits by structure, sealed targets, and four separate statuses. The G split (held-out bare shapes, deeper eval) is a fair test of neural generalisation. The path breaks in three places. First, every task built so far (Helm's graph questions, G, R, A, C) is generated by one of the project's own fixed programs from the very input the learner sees. So a pass can only show imitation plus transfer. The one mode where the fixed program is not the ceiling is native interpretation from language, which is scheduled 'later'. The data generator (SDG) runs CAS to English only. Second, Q6 would plug CAS modules into Helm's recurrent messages. Yet measured Helm answers do not depend on those messages (R2-F1), and its world scorer cannot compare worlds (R2-F5). Third, R1 shares no component with the pointer machine: no ^6 block, no rounds, no graph input. Lab results would not test the Helm 1.0/2.0 machine.

solo.name: Gate forensics (WHY HELM 1.0 / 2.0 DID NOT PASS)
solo.summary_plain: Helm 1.0 "passed" because it went from 0 to 2 right answers to 11 or 12 right, out of 18 frozen test questions. The gate compares each run with its own untrained starting point. But a rule that learns nothing (the "floor") already answers 11 of those 18. In every seed, Helm 1.0 had exactly 2 right answers beyond the floor, and they were always the same two reach questions. So the pass mostly measured "climbed from a random start up to the floor". A machine that only copied the floor rule would also have passed, at odds of 1 in 2048. Helm 2.0's failing label came from one seed only (20260919), not two. The real rule does not say "no losses". It needs more gains than losses and an exact chance value of 1/100 or less, so one loss raises the bar from 7 gains to 10. Seed 20260917 passed with 11 gains and 1 loss. Seed 20260919 failed with 7 gains and 1 loss (chance value 9/256): its untrained start already had 4 right, and one reach question turned wrong only at the very last checkpoint. The lineage file, the audit pack, the audit report and trusted_rescore.py all state the rule wrongly as "0 broken". In substance, 2.0 is not better than 1.0 on these 18 questions: its final answers match 1.0's exactly in two seeds and are one worse in the third. Its one real gain (correspondence: 0 to 20 of 20 answers on unseen worlds) is invisible to the gate by design. Outside that gain it is slightly worse on reach, on parts, and on the memory check in two seeds. My answer is both: the failure itself is brittle, but a pass would not have shown that 2.0 is better either.

findings.claim: Only ONE of Helm 2.0's three seeds failed the frozen gate. One right-to-wrong flip does NOT fail a seed. The registered rule is b > c (b = questions wrong at the start and right at the end, c = right at the start and wrong at the end), plus an exact one-sided binomial chance value of 1/100 or less, plus gains in at least 2 kinds and at least 2 worlds. With c = 0 a seed needs at least 7 gains. With c = 1 it needs at least 10. Seed 20260917 had b=11, c=1, chance value 13/4096 = 0.003173828125, so it PASSED. Seed 20260918 had b=12, c=0, chance value 1/4096, so it PASSED. Seed 20260919 had b=7, c=1, chance value 9/256 = 0.03515625 > 1/100, so it FAILED. The label needs all three seeds to pass, so it printed NO_TRANSFER_TO_NEW_WORLDS. With c = 0, the same 7 gains would have given 1/128 = 0.0078125 and a pass.

findings.claim: Many project records misstate the gate rule as 'broken must be 0'. BRAIN_LINEAGE.md even misquotes the frozen reading: it says seed 20260917 was False, but the reading says True. trusted_rescore.py puts the wrong rule into code. For Helm 2.0 its reading reports seed 20260917 passed=false, while the frozen reading it claims to agree with says True. solo.name: Code forensics (WHY Q4 GOT 0/16: the code)
solo.summary_plain: I found no code bug that explains the 0/16. The encoder's summary vector does reach the decoder, both in training and at test time. My scan of every Q4 learner file and the job script found no variable that is set and then ignored in the learning path. So this is not a repeat of Helm 1.0's unused 'block' variable. Instead, the model stopped while it was still learning the average answer. That average does not depend on the input. Its loss never beat a simple counting rule that ignores the input (0 of the last 32 updates). The single tree it printed has the shape and choices of the most common training answer: one PLUS joining two plain states, with no drive and no register. The decoder follows the model's scores honestly. When I fed it the correct scores, the program and the checker gave 16/16. The main causes are design limits. The run had 128 single-example updates (the code does not allow more). The input vector enters the decoder only once, as its starting state. And the test examples are all depth 3 with tree shapes never seen in training, so anything that ignores the input scores 0.

findings.claim: The architecture makes the input signal weak early in training. First, the encoder vector enters the decoder only as its initial hidden state; it is not fed at every step, and there is no attention. This is deliberate, because it is the strict bottleneck. Second, the encoder reads left to right and keeps only its final state. The first input-dependent decision after BINARY and the operator is whether the root's left child is a tree. That fact sits in byte index 1, the byte farthest from the encoder's final state. Even the cue nearest the final state went unused. Verdict: DESIGN_LIMIT.

open_questions.question: On the saved checkpoint, are the 16 dev bottleneck vectors actually different from each other? And does the decoder's first input-dependent logit gap (STATE vs BINARY at step 2) change at all across the 16 inputs?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It separates two explanations. Either the encoder gives nearly the same vector for every input, or the decoder ignores its starting state. It would confirm or refute R4-F2 and R4-F7 directly, instead of by inference from loss curves.

open_questions.question: Can this exact pipeline (same code, width 64, lr 0.001) overfit a tiny fixed set, for example 8 training rows repeated for a few hundred updates, until it reconstructs those 8 exactly?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It is the standard test for hidden defects. If it cannot overfit 8 rows, there is a defect I did not find by reading. If it can, the 0/16 is budget and design, not code.
open_questions.how_to_test: One short bounded run on the local RTX 4070 under a new plan with a repeated 8-row subset. Report exact reconstruction on those 8 rows and whether the outputs differ from each other.

solo.name: Data and outputs forensics (WHY Q4 GOT 0/16: the evidence)
solo.summary_plain: The model never learned to read its input. Every one of the 128 logged training losses sits above a guesser that looks at no input. That guesser only knows which kind of token comes next and how often each value appears. The saved output (^7^E + ^7^C) is exactly the tree a no-input guesser writes when it picks the most likely token at each step. The one difference is the two leaf labels, and there the training data is almost perfectly even. That guesser always stops after two leaves. So it writes 13 tokens, but the 16 dev answers need 27 to 55 tokens. The dev test also uses only tree shapes that never appear in training. So any answer copied from training scores 0/16. This covers every training tree, the modal tree, a nearest-neighbour lookup, and a leaf-copy into a training shape. A 20-line bracket parser I wrote scores 16/16, and the record gives the compiler 1.0 on the harder eval split. The loss was still falling at the last update, with no flat part yet. The run was built as an engineering test, capped at 128 single-example updates. It stopped before the model could learn even the no-input guesser. So 0/16 shows the training budget was far too small. It does not show that this architecture cannot learn. The run saved no example ids. I rebuilt the 128 rows from the seed: all 128 are different, out of 2,048. A shuffle control strongly supports that rebuild.

findings.claim: No output shape seen in training can ever be right on the dev records. Dev tree shapes are held out whole: train has 16 bare shapes, dev has 9, and 0 are shared. All 2,048 training trees are different from one another (most repeated count = 1). So 'always output the most common training tree' is a 2,048-way tie. Every baseline that reuses a training shape scores 0/16 exact: training row 0, the modal depth-1 tree (^4^O + ^4^O), the modal depth-3 skeleton, R0 byte-bag nearest neighbour, and leaf-copy into the modal training shape. Only reading the brackets from the input works. R5's 20-line bracket-and-literal parser matches 16/16 saved reference ASTs. The recorded compiler reference scores 1.0 on G eval.

findings.claim: The constant output is the tree a no-input guesser writes when it picks the most likely token at each step. I built an input-blind prior, B3: it knows the grammar slot and the node depth, but never sees the input. I decoded it greedily through the same grammar mask and lowest-id tie rule. It writes (^4^O + ^4^O): BINARY, PLUS, then two STATE leaves, each with F_NONE and REG_ABSENT, then EOS. That is 13 tokens, the same skeleton as the model's (^7^E + ^7^C). The two differ only at 4 token positions: noetic N7 vs N4 (twice), and domain D_E/D_C vs D_O. In training, those two fields are almost perfectly even. The guesser stops at two leaves because at node depth 1, STATE (0.592529) beats BINARY (0.407471). All 16 dev targets are depth 3, with 27-55 tokens. So any decoder that ignores its input scores 0/16 here by construction.

findings.claim: The training budget was far too small for this task. The job code allows at most 128 updates and at most 2,048 training rows. Each update uses one example, with AdamW at learning rate 0.001 and clip 1.0. The README calls it an engineering smoke. The model has 70,818 learned parameters but saw only 2,553 target tokens (about 27.7 parameters per token). The whole input must pass through one 64-number vector (the GRU's last hidden state). From that vector the decoder must rebuild 27-55 tokens in an unseen shape. Leaf content alone is about 10.643856 bits per leaf, so about 85 bits for 8 leaves. The model's loss gap above the no-input guesser B3 shrank from 1.631901-1.813058 (updates 1-64) to 0.737633-0.827027 (updates 65-128). Depth-3 rows had the largest gap (0.827027). Reading: the run stopped before the model reached the no-input guesser level. Rebuilding an input needs a loss below that level. So 0/16 shows the budget was too small; it does not show the architecture cannot learn. The evidence cannot say how many updates would be enough. A straight-line guess (about 44 more updates just to reach B2) is crude.

solo.name: Lineage pattern analyst (WHY THE LINE KEEPS NOT PASSING)
solo.summary_plain: Across the whole line, the test often failed the brain as much as the brain failed the test. The frozen 18-question test was both too easy and too fragile at once. A "floor" here means the score of a rule that learns nothing. On those 18 questions the floor is 11. Also, losing one question means the brain needs three more gains to pass. Helm 1.0 passed right at that floor. The reason was a coding slip: its eight reasoning rounds never read their own state, so they acted as one round. The pre-run reviews never checked the built loop for that. Helm 2.0 fixed the loop and got real gains, including correspondence 0 to 20 of 20. The 18-question test could not count that gain, and the brain failed on one seed after losing one question. The earlier practice study failed for a different reason: its input could not describe a world the brain had never practised. That was found only after the run. Today's Q4 smoke ran just 128 tiny training steps and was scored only on tree shapes it had never seen. It printed the most common training shape for every input. Most of these problems except the loop slip and the input problem were predicted in writing before the runs. Those predictions did not reach the pass rule or the result write-up. Process problems also cost runs and caused wrong statements: many agents editing shared branches, runs killed mid-flight, and smoke runs read as experiments. One record error: the lineage file says Helm 2.0 seed 20260917 failed, but the frozen grader says it passed. The label is the same either way.

findings.claim: The instrument in use was repeatedly passable by a no-learning rule. It was both too easy and too fragile. Helm 1.0: the one-hop plus rank rules solve 11 of the frozen 18 questions. That floor was computed and pinned by a test on 2026-09-19 11:34, before certification on 2026-09-20 06:05. But the gate compares against the untrained start, not the floor (b > c, p <= 0.01). So a machine that learned only the one-hop rule could pass, and Helm 1.0 did: 12/12/11, which is 2/2/2 answers beyond the floor at p = 0.50/0.50/0.69. The same pattern appears in the practice study: the input-blind reach->DIRECT shortcut was the only held-back gain. It appears again in Q3 v0.1: a hand rule scored 1.000000, a train lookup scored 1.000000, a regex reproduced 204/256, and C dev was 102/256 verbatim in train. PREDICTED before the run for Helm 1.0 but not made the pass condition. Q3's cases were caught before any training.

findings.claim: Today's Q4 0/16 is best explained by three things. First, a tiny training budget. Second, a readout only on never-seen tree shapes. Third, no success rule written in advance. The model got 128 single-example AdamW updates at lr 0.001 on 128 of 2,048 rows, and 73 of 128 updates hit the clip. Loss started near the uniform value ln(34) = 3.5263605246161616 and was still falling steeply at the end. The only accuracy readout was the dev split. By design, the dev split holds out whole tree shapes: 9 dev shapes, 16 train shapes, 0 shared. No training-row reconstruction was measured. The single output, (^7^E + ^7^C), has shape (x + x). That is the most common shape in the 128 rows actually trained (44 of 128). All dev rows are depth 3 (256/256). INFERRED from this: the decoder learned the output prior, not an input-to-output mapping. The acceptance vector V26 sets no threshold, and the runbook states no expected accuracy, so NOT predicted in writing. The designed experiment was a depth sweep against a bag-plus-nearest-neighbour baseline. The executed smoke measured one depth, 16 records, and no baseline.

(1) Shortcuts and leaks in v0.1: refusals recycled, a hand rule and a lookup at 1.0, the R shape acting as a fingerprint, and C dev not deduplicated. (4) Concurrency: another checkout rewrote the v0.5 pins in place. Each break was caught by review before any learner trained on it. So the Q3 churn did not cause a failed run. It does show that the builder's first claims about the data are unreliable until attacked.

solo.name: Contrarian (the strongest case against the easy stories)
solo.summary_plain: Most of the easy stories hold up, but three of them are worded wrongly. "Q4 failed" is a category error. Nothing written before the run set an accuracy target for this smoke test. The smoke was also declared "claim_bearing": false. The accurate wording is: the engineering run completed, and its accuracy result was negative. The 0/16 is what an under-trained model gives. By update 128 its training loss was still worse than a model that ignores the input and only knows the usual answer shapes (worse on 32 of the last 32 updates). Its one repeated answer matches the most common tokens in the examples it trained on. The dev test also used only tree shapes that never appear in training, so 0/16 cannot tell "cannot learn" apart from "cannot handle new shapes". "Q4 is Helm" is false: the Q4 network is a separate 70,818-parameter byte-GRU (a small recurrent network that reads raw bytes) and imports no Helm code. Helm itself was not run today. The reconstruction task is exact parsing. My 20-line parser gets 16/16, so success could only show that a learned representation keeps structure. It could never beat the compiler. For Helm 2.0, the contrarian case mostly fails. Its whole gain on the 127 held-back answers comes from one kind, correspondence. On the other kinds combined it scored lower than Helm 1.0 on all three seeds. The contrarian case is right about one thing. The 18-question gate has almost no resolving power: only 2 of its questions can be won above the zero-learning floor without analogy, and all 6 runs got exactly those 2. The lineage file states the gate rule wrongly (it says zero broken questions are required). Under the frozen grader's own rule, Helm 2.0 missed on one seed by one question. "Helm 1.0 passed" is true only as a grader printout. It beat its own untrained start, not a rule that learns nothing.

new_evidence.claim: Helm cannot do analogy as built, and the saved predictions prove it. In every trained run (Helm 1.0 and 2.0, all three seeds), Helm gives the SAME world as its answer to all 70 analogy records. The code explains why. For an analogy question, the query holds no information about the focus world. Each world's vector is built from that world alone. So every candidate world except the focus gets the same score whatever the focus is. The model can only rank the worlds in one fixed order and skip the focus when it is on top. The 16 of 70 whole-course analogy answers counted as correct are records where that one fixed world happens to be admissible. The held 0 of 17 follows by construction. This turns R2-F5 from INFERRED into a measured result plus a code proof. It also means 5 of the frozen 18 gate questions could not be won by either version.

dispute.reason: Minor, and it does not change the conclusion. The INFERRED sentence 'each weight moves at most about lr per step' is a typical size, not a bound. For Adam with default betas (0.9, 0.999), the published bound on one step is lr * (1 - beta1) / sqrt(1 - beta2), about 3.16 * lr. So 128 steps allow a worst-case move of about 0.40, not 0.128. The usual step is still about lr, so 'few updates' stands.

new_evidence.claim: The reasoning loop is a weak channel by design, in both Helm versions. That design fact links R2-F1's ablations to the question of whether the F1 loop repair could ever have mattered. Each round adds only PER_ROUND_UPDATE_CAP (0.01) x tanh(round_rate) x update to the node state, which is then renormalised. round_rate starts at exactly 0, so at initialisation the loop does nothing at all. The same capped write is in Helm 1.0. The update is merge x [tanh, tanh] (core_block), so the 0.01 is relative to a learnable weight norm, not a hard limit. Measured with Helm 1.0's trained weights, the effect of a change two hops away was 0.0018496513366699219. Resetting the whole round group barely moves the held-back score. So even a correctly wired loop may carry little signal unless training grows round_rate and the merge weights. The trained round_rate is not recorded in any JSON I opened.

consensus.statement: What 'pass' meant, and what Helm 1.0's pass measured. The frozen grader passes a seed when b > c, exact one-sided binomial p <= 1/100, gains in >= 2 kinds and >= 2 worlds, where b counts questions wrong at the untrained start and right at the end and c counts the reverse. The label LEARNS_NEW_WORLDS needs all three seeds. The reference is the run's own untrained start, not a no-learning rule. Helm 1.0 (b/c 10/0, 12/0, 11/0) passed. But the registered one-hop + rank-last floor (pinned by a test on 2026-09-19 11:34, before certification on 2026-09-20 06:05) already answers 11 of the frozen 18. Helm 1.0's net score against that floor is +1, +1, 0 (it answered 2 non-floor questions in every seed and missed 1, 1, 2 floor questions). A machine that knew only the one-hop rule would have passed (b 7, c 0, p 1/128).

consensus.statement: Q4: the single repeated tree (^7^E + ^7^C) is the input-blind prior skeleton. Its 8 structural tokens (BINARY, PLUS, STATE x2, F_NONE x2, REG_ABSENT x2) are strict majorities of the training targets, and the input-blind prior stops at two leaves because at node depth 1 STATE beats BINARY. Against any-depth majorities it matches 9 of 12 content tokens. The leaf labels are near-ties: a count model over the 128 seen rows with each token weighted 1/len (as the job's per-example loss weights it) decodes (^7^E + ^7^E), 12 of 13 tokens equal. Other reasonable count models give other labels, so the exact labels are not firmly explained (OPEN).

consensus.statement: Common root (pattern across the line). (1) Results were read against weak references: the untrained start instead of the no-learning floor (Helm 1.0/2.0), the cheapest correspondence baseline (4/20) instead of the strongest (20/20), no constant-ABSENT line on the ten-node panel, and no input-blind floor in Q4. (2) A recurring defect class: a part exists but its consumer never reads or receives it (Helm 1.0 'block'; the unwired F4 schedule; the analogy scorer that never sees the focus world; the rescorer that never compares per-seed pass bits); tests check wiring, not effect. (3) Every task built so far (Helm's graph questions, Q3 G/A/C/R) has an exact answer computable by the project's own fixed programs from the model's visible input, so a pass could only show imitation plus transfer, not learning beyond those programs. (4) Process: many agents on shared branches, killed runs and in-place edits cost evidence (Helm 0.1 uncertifiable). 'Memorising' is a symptom where the input or head cannot express the rule, not a separate cause.

research_tasks.question: Forward-only diagnostic of the saved Q4 checkpoint: does its output depend on its input, where does input information stop, and can it rebuild training-type rows?
research_tasks.how_to_test: GPU task 1 of 2, run first. Local RTX 4070, inference only, no training, results to SCRATCH/RT1 only, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1. Load records/q4_authorized_20260922/run_001/checkpoint (weights sha256 d54f57155a54cbd28621d92af9cb5f45e425c015a559cf80103966ccbf275477) with q4_checkpoint.load_checkpoint on cuda:0. (0) Sanity: re-decode the 16 dev inputs with free_decode and compare with run_001/dev_predictions.jsonl. (1) encode() the 16 dev inputs, the 128 seen rows (random.Random(20260921).shuffle(range(2048))[:128]; list SCRATCH/R5/used_rows.json) and 128 unseen train rows; report relative spread = mean pairwise L2 distance / mean vector norm. (2) For each dev input, next_logits after prefixes [BINARY] and [BINARY, PLUS] with true, zeroed and swapped (another input's) bottleneck; report logit[TIMES]-logit[PLUS] and logit[BINARY]-logit[STATE], and the fraction of inputs whose full greedy decode changes under swap/zero. (3) Free-decode the 128 seen and 128 unseen train rows; score canonical-exact by depth with the dict-equality checker (q4_smoke_job.py:388); count distinct outputs. (4) Teacher-forced mean cross-entropy on those rows and the 16 dev targets, beside the SCRATCH/R5 input-blind learners (online bigram, loss-weighted slot prior) on the same rows.
research_tasks.outcome_rules: Written before running. (a) If step 0 does not reproduce all 16 saved predictions exactly -> BUG in checkpoint save/load or decoding; stop and report. (b) If relative spread < 0.05 on dev and seen rows -> ENCODER COLLAPSE: the vector carries almost no input information. (c) If spread >= 0.05 but swap/zero changes the greedy decode on 0 of 16 inputs and every |logit gap change| < 0.1 -> DECODER IGNORES THE BOTTLENECK. (d) If swap/zero changes decodes on >= 2 of 16 or logit gaps shift by >= 0.5 -> input is used but too weakly to leave the prior. (e) If seen-row exact >= 1 at any depth -> the pipeline can map input to output; no gross BUG. (f) If seen and unseen train rows are 0 exact with 1-2 distinct outputs and teacher-forced CE on them is >= the input-blind CE on the same rows -> consistent with TOO LITTLE TRAINING; bug not excluded, go to RT2. Neither (b) nor (c) alone is a code defect; both are expected states of an under-trained strict bottleneck. None of these outcomes changes any claim status; results are scratch-only diagnostics.
research_tasks.settles: D2; part of D1 (bug vs not-yet-trained)

research_tasks.question: With a larger bounded budget, does the same R1 pipeline fit and generalise to training-type shapes while held-out shapes stay at 0? This separates BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs TASK/DESIGN LIMIT.
research_tasks.how_to_test: GPU task 2 of 2, run only after RT1 (skip if RT1 hits outcome (a)). One bounded diagnostic re-run on the local RTX 4070: at most 2,000 updates and at most 5 minutes wall time (stop at whichever comes first and report the count), results in SCRATCH/RT2 only, no commit, non-claim-bearing. Do NOT edit q4_smoke_job.py (its cap is 128); write a scratch driver that imports the lab modules read-only with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1. Same StrictR1 width 64, seed 20260921, AdamW lr 0.001, clip 1.0, one example per update, same loss. Train by cycling over a fixed subset S = the first 256 rows of random.Random(20260921).shuffle(range(2048)) (about 8 passes). Evaluate at updates 500, 1000 and the end: (i) canonical-exact on S by depth; (ii) canonical-exact on 128 train rows not in S whose bare shape occurs in S, by depth; (iii) canonical-exact on dev rows 1-16 and all 256 dev rows; (iv) number of distinct outputs per set; (v) teacher-forced CE on set (ii) vs the online bigram and loss-weighted slot prior on the same rows.
research_tasks.outcome_rules: Written before running. BUG (or broken optimisation): at the end, S exact at depth 1 < 10% AND distinct outputs on S <= 2 AND CE on S not below the input-blind prior on S -> the pipeline cannot fit 256 rows in about 8 passes; report as BUG_OR_OPTIMISATION_FAILURE and propose an 8-row overfit test next round. TOO LITTLE TRAINING (for the smoke): S exact > 0 and set (ii) exact > 0 at depths 1-2, with outputs varying by input -> the 128-update constant output is explained by budget. TASK/DESIGN LIMIT at this budget: set (ii) depth-3 exact >= 25% while dev exact = 0 of 256 -> the model reconstructs seen shapes but not held-out shapes; the 0/16 reflects shape/length extrapolation under the strict bottleneck, not only budget (not proof of impossibility at larger budgets). SHAPE TRANSFER POSSIBLE: dev exact >= 1 of 256 -> held-out shapes are reachable and the smoke's 0/16 was budget. Mixed results (e.g. set (ii) depth-3 between 0 and 25%, dev 0) -> INCONCLUSIVE; report numbers only. If the 5-minute cap stops the run before 2,000 updates, apply the rules to the updates reached and mark BUDGET_LIMITED.
research_tasks.settles: D1 (BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs TASK/DESIGN LIMIT for Q4)

research_tasks.question: What are the trained values of round_rate (and round_mix) in the six Helm final checkpoints, i.e. how open is the reasoning loop after training?
research_tasks.how_to_test: Read-only, no torch import. For receipt_2026091{7,8,9}/checkpoints and receipt_helm1_certified_2026091{7,8,9}/checkpoints final.pt and initial.pt: open as a zip with zipfile, unpickle data.pkl with a custom pickle.Unpickler whose find_class stubs torch._utils._rebuild_tensor_v2 and torch storage classes, then read the raw little-endian float32 bytes of the round_rate (1 value) and round_mix entries from the archive's data/<key> members. Report g = 0.01 x tanh(round_rate) per run. PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, output to SCRATCH/RT3.
research_tasks.outcome_rules: Written before running. If unpickling needs anything beyond stubbing tensor/storage rebuilds -> UNREADABLE_WITHOUT_TORCH; stop, report, defer. If |g| < 0.001 in all six runs -> the loop is nearly shut after training; the design cap, not only the 1.0 wiring defect, keeps rounds weak (supports R7-N4). If |g| >= 0.005 in all three Helm 2.0 runs -> the loop is open; the ablation insensitivity means answers route around it (heads and input side-channels). Otherwise -> MIXED; report values. This is one factor only; the merge weights also scale the update, so no outcome alone proves the loop carries or lacks signal.

research_tasks.question: Does Helm's reach head choose its VIA node by the structural rule (common neighbour of whole and part) or by node-local cues? And do untrained models carry a built-in bias that makes each seed's gate result a start-point lottery?
research_tasks.how_to_test: Read-only pure JSON. For all six receipts, course_p00 and course_p10 predictions/scoring plus the six ablation_*_predictions.json, and world edges and declarations from records/typed_course_001/checks_002/public_course.json (public bank only; never sealed or private_targets files). For every reach record answered VIA, compare the chosen node with each cue: common neighbour (lexfirst), rank-last non-argument, rank-first non-argument, part's parent, node with both a parent and a child, highest declared participant rank. Report agreement overall and on records where the common-neighbour cue disagrees with each node-local cue. Separately, at p00, report per run the share of pointed reach/parts nodes that are rank-last vs 1/(nodes minus 2), and which frozen floor questions each untrained start already answers.
research_tasks.outcome_rules: Written before running. If there are fewer than 5 cue-disagreement records -> INCONCLUSIVE for the structural question. If on disagreement records the p10 VIA node equals the common neighbour in >= 80% and each node-local cue in <= 30% -> STRUCTURAL local rule (supports R3-N3). If it equals some single node-local cue in >= 80% -> SHORTCUT (supports R6's concern). Otherwise -> MIXED. For the start-point question: if untrained starts point at the rank-last node at >= 2x the chance rate in >= 4 of 6 runs -> built-in start-point lottery on rank-last floor questions (supports R7-N1 reading); if within 1.5x chance in all runs -> no systematic bias; the 20260919 start was chance.

research_tasks.question: Why does Helm miss DIRECT (0-7 of 8) and parts (0-1 of 6) on the ten-node panel when a one-hop rule answers both exactly? Is it an input-range shift from four-node to ten-node worlds?

chairStates.decision_reason: Most answers are settled and heavily cross-checked by independent measurements. WHY HELM is settled from the record; the one gap is why the word 'Helm' was chosen, and only the owner can answer that. Helm 1.0 passed only against its untrained start, and zero-learning programs answer every frozen question. Helm 2.0 failed on one seed, after one flip at the last checkpoint, from a lucky untrained start; the gate rule is misquoted in the records. The Q4 0/16 is a negative observation without a preset target. The key Q4 split is still open: BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs TASK/DESIGN LIMIT. Today it rests on inference from losses and code reading. No one has run an overfit test, a training-shape readout, or an input-sensitivity check. RT1 (forward-only on the saved checkpoint) and RT2 (a bounded re-run with a training-shape readout) can change that answer materially. RT3 and RT4 are cheap read-only tasks that settle the loop-openness and reach-cue disputes. The remaining disputes (D3, D4) are owner decisions, not research tasks. D6 and D7 need Helm GPU runs outside this round's allowance.

consensus.statement: WHY HELM (origin). Helm is the learning part of the CNCM pointer machine. It exists because the machine before it (the typed practice study) failed in a measured way. consensus.statement: WHY HELM (design choices). Pointer answers make the skill world-independent. The input was changed to read one world as a directed graph with no words (node identity = registered rank), because pointer answers alone could not work. The gate was keyed on the RELATIONAL kinds because a pure flag copier passed the older gate (b = 10, c = 0, p = 0.0009765625). The protocol warned before the run that the gate had low power (P(all three seeds clear) 0.0216 / 0.2450 / 0.6839 at a true 30% / 40% / 50% improvement), and the owner chose to 'Run it as the transfer test, label honestly'. The cost of the no-words choice: every relational answer is a short graph program of the input. Refinement from round 1: nodes are ADDRESSED by rank, but with node_rank_feature False the node rows carry no rank value (the rank column is replaced by is_primary_label); only the whole/part argument ranks enter, as raw numbers in the query vector (RT5-F2). So two nodes with the same graph position and flags cannot be told apart by rank.

consensus.statement: Common root (pattern across the line). (1) Results were read against weak references (untrained start instead of the no-learning floor; cheapest correspondence baseline; no input-blind floor in Q4), while stronger references written before the runs never reached the pass rule. (2) A recurring defect class: a part exists but its consumer never reads it; tests check wiring, not effect. (3) Every task built so far has an exact answer computable by the project's own fixed programs from the model's visible input. RT6 confirms this for the whole plan as written (Q0-Q6): 9362/9362 visible Q3 records, 61/61 operation contract cases and 1072/1072 ladder answers are computed by reference programs; 'native interpretation' has no task id and no phase. Caveat: T16 has not frozen its Q5 families, so a new family would need a new decision. A future Q4/Helm 3.0 pass could show imitation plus transfer to new shapes, not learning beyond those programs. (4) Process: shared branches, killed runs and in-place edits cost evidence. The claim is INFERRED as a pattern; its parts are measured.

disputes.statement: Q4 0/16: is the cause a BUG in the learning path, TOO LITTLE TRAINING, or a TASK/DESIGN LIMIT (strict 64-number final-state bottleneck fed only as the decoder's starting state; left-to-right encoder that loses the input's start)? Narrowed in round 1: the checkpoint, decoder, checker, save/load and training replay are cleared (C16); the constant output is a budget effect (C29); but at 15.625x the updates on 256 rows the model still gets 0 exact, even depth-1 rows trained 7-8 times, and learns tree shape without leaf content (C29). No RT2 rule covered this state.
disputes.sides: Too-little-training side: loss still falling (1.065938 in pass 8, drop 0.00904), and a 70,818-parameter GRU at lr 0.001 may simply learn leaf copying slowly. Design side (RT1-F11, RT2-F9): the encoder keeps mainly the input's end and the decoder barely reads input-specific content (+0.000460 logits), so leaf content may not pass the bottleneck. Bug side: 0 correct leaf sequences on 105 single-leaf rows seen 7-8 times is surprising for a copy task (C19: the input is the expression string), and no overfit test has been run.
disputes.what_would_settle_it: RT7 (8-row overfit re-run with per-slot and TRUE-vs-SWAP readouts) and RT8 (full scripted-gold replay of the grammar mask over all 2,304 visible train+dev rows).

research_tasks.question: Can the unchanged Q4 pipeline memorise 8 training rows exactly? And if not, does it fail on leaf content only, with the decoder ignoring row-specific bottleneck content? This separates BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs DESIGN LIMIT for D1.
research_tasks.how_to_test: The only GPU task this round (the one bounded diagnostic re-run). Local RTX 4070, at most 2,000 updates and at most 5 minutes wall time, results in SCRATCH/RT7 only, no commit, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, repo untouched. Reuse the RT2 scratch driver (SCRATCH/RT2/rt2_run.py, bit-faithful per RT2-F1) with one change: S8 = the first 8 rows of random.Random(20260921).shuffle(range(2048)) (the smoke's first 8 rows). Same StrictR1 width 64, seed 20260921, AdamW lr 0.001, clip 1.0, one example per update, same loss, cycling S8 for 2000 updates (250 passes). Targets from the R5 parser on visible observations (validated 2048/2048). Fidelity pre-check: the first 8 losses must equal updates 1-8 of run_001/updates.jsonl. Evaluate at 250, 500, 1000 and 2000 updates: (i) free-decode exact on S8 (dict equality, q4_smoke_job.py:388), with each row's depth; (ii) teacher-forced argmax token accuracy on S8 per slot class (expr, op, noetic, domain, drive, register, eos); (iii) teacher-forced CE on S8 per slot class with the TRUE bottleneck and with a SWAPPED bottleneck (row (i+1) mod 8's vector); (iv) bottleneck relative spread on S8 (RT1 definition); (v) mean training loss per 8-update pass. For context only (not a rule input): free-decode dev rows 1-16 at the end.
research_tasks.outcome_rules: Written before running. (0) If the fidelity pre-check fails -> SCRIPT_DEFECT; stop and report; no reading. If the 5-minute cap stops the run early -> BUDGET_LIMITED; apply the rules to the updates reached. Rules are read at the final evaluation. (A) FITS: S8 exact >= 7 of 8 -> no gross defect in the learning path; the pipeline can carry leaf content through the 64-number state for 8 rows; RT2's 0/256 is then a rate or capacity issue at 256 rows (TOO LITTLE TRAINING or capacity DESIGN LIMIT), not a BUG. (B) BUG_OR_OPTIMISATION_FAILURE: S8 exact <= 1 of 8 AND pooled leaf-slot (noetic+domain+drive+register) teacher-forced accuracy on S8 < 50% AND last-pass mean training loss > 0.5 -> a 70,818-parameter model cannot memorise 8 rows in 250 passes; recommend a code audit of the leaf path, not more training. (C) BOTTLENECK_NOT_USED: S8 exact <= 1 of 8 AND structure-slot (expr+op+eos) teacher-forced accuracy >= 95% AND pooled leaf-slot CE with SWAP minus CE with TRUE < 0.05 nats -> even under memorisation pressure the decoder learns shared structure but does not read row-specific content from the bottleneck; points to a DESIGN limit of the strict final-state bottleneck at this lr (or a defect in the bottleneck path), not to budget. If (B) and (C) both fire, report both; (C) is the more specific reading. (D) Otherwise (for example 2-6 of 8 exact) -> INCONCLUSIVE; report numbers only; D1 stays open. All results DIAGNOSTIC_NOT_CLAIM_BEARING; none changes any claim status.
research_tasks.settles: D1 (BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs DESIGN LIMIT)

chairStates.decision_reason: Round 1 settled most of the open questions. The facts behind D2 and D8 are now in consensus (C23, C28). D5 and D6 were narrowed (C24, C25, C11). The ten-node panel and the plan map were read under their fixed rules (C26, C21, C27). One key question is still open and can still move: D1, the Q4 split between a code defect, too little training, and a design limit. RT2 fit none of its fixed outcomes. After 2000 updates the model learned tree shape but got 0 leaves right. It even missed single-leaf rows it had trained on 7 or 8 times. The input is the expression string itself, so this is surprising. The cleanest missing check is an 8-row overfit test (RT7), the one GPU re-run allowed. It has outcome rules that separate 'cannot memorise' (points to a defect), 'memorises structure but ignores row-specific content' (points to a design limit) and 'fits' (points to budget or capacity). RT8 is a $0 check that clears or finds a mask or codec defect on every visible row. RT9 is a $0 check on whether Helm's one open loop is used. D3, D4, D9, D10 and D11 are owner decisions, not research. D5, D6 and D7 need GPU runs on Helm weights, which this meeting's allowance does not include. All GPU numbers are DIAGNOSTIC_NOT_CLAIM_BEARING. No claim status is changed; these findings are advice to the owner.

consensus.statement: WHY HELM (design choices). Pointer answers make the skill world-independent. The input was changed to read one world as a directed graph with no words (node identity = registered rank), because pointer answers alone could not work. The gate was keyed on the RELATIONAL kinds because a pure flag copier passed the older gate (b = 10, c = 0, p = 0.0009765625). The protocol warned before the run that the gate had low power (P(all three seeds clear) 0.0216 / 0.2450 / 0.6839 at a true 30% / 40% / 50% improvement), and the owner chose to 'Run it as the transfer test, label honestly'. The cost of the no-words choice: every relational answer is a short graph program of the input. Nodes are ADDRESSED by rank, but with node_rank_feature False the node rows carry no rank value (the rank column is replaced by is_primary_label); only the whole/part argument ranks enter, as raw numbers in the query vector (RT5-F2). So two nodes with the same graph position and flags cannot be told apart by rank.

consensus.statement: Common root (pattern across the line). (1) Results were read against weak references (untrained start instead of the no-learning floor; cheapest correspondence baseline; no input-blind floor in Q4), while stronger references written before the runs never reached the pass rule. (2) A recurring defect class: a part exists but its consumer never reads it; tests check wiring, not effect. (3) Every task built so far has an exact answer computable by the project's own fixed programs from the model's visible input. RT6 confirms this for the whole plan as written (Q0-Q6): 9362/9362 visible Q3 records, 61/61 operation contract cases and 1072/1072 ladder answers are computed by reference programs; 'native interpretation' has no task id and no phase. (4) Process: shared branches, killed runs and in-place edits cost evidence. (5) Round 2 adds a benchmark-design point: the Helm course bank barely exercises multi-step reach (RT9-F8, RT9-F10), so a loop repair could not show a gain there. disputes.statement: Q4 0/16, narrowed after round 2: the BUG side is excluded at the level tested (mask and codec on all 2304 visible rows, C30; learning path memorises 8 rows, C31). What remains open is TOO LITTLE TRAINING (rate) vs a capacity DESIGN LIMIT of the strict 64-number final-state bottleneck at 256+ rows, and whether this design can learn a general leaf-copy skill at all (RT7 memorised; dev 0/16).
disputes.sides: Rate side (RT7-F8, INFERRED): RT2's 7.8125 showings per row is far before the 125 showings at which 8 rows fit, and RT2's loss was still falling. Capacity/design side (RT1-F11, RT2-F9): a left-to-right GRU that hands over only its final 64 numbers may saturate before 256 rows of leaf content fit; RT2's dev CE was above the input-blind slot prior. Neither is tested at 256 rows.
disputes.what_would_settle_it: An owner-authorised longer run on RT2's 256-row set (about 32,000 updates, comparable showings per row to RT7's fit), with outcome rules written first: exact >= most rows on S -> rate; plateau with 0 exact and leaf SWAP-minus-TRUE near 0 -> capacity limit. Then a held-out test on shapes seen in training (RT2 set (ii)) to separate memorisation from a leaf-copy skill. This exceeds the meeting's 2,000-update cap.

disputes.statement: Which zero-learning floor defines what a Helm result is read against: the registered one-hop + rank-last set (11 of 18), that set plus the pre-run LB18 analogy rule (16 of 18), or also the post-hoc one-step VIA / mirror-rank rules (18 of 18)?

disputes.what_would_settle_it: An owner- or evaluation-custodian-signed record naming the floor rule set, then a pure-Python re-read of both frozen gate readings. Not a research question; Claude does not decide it.

disputes.statement: Which per-seed pass rule governs the Helm gate: the frozen grader's (b > c, exact p <= 1/100) or the rescorer's (>= 7 gained, 0 lost)?

disputes.what_would_settle_it: Owner-signed record naming one rule; then a $0 unit test of both rule functions on synthetic (10,1)/(12,0)/(12,0) flags to confirm the rescorer's behaviour (C14).

disputes.statement: Does Helm pick its 2-hop VIA node by the two-sided structural rule (common neighbour of whole and part), or by a one-sided node cue ('a parent of the part' or 'a node with both a parent and a child')? It follows the unique common neighbour 266/270 and does not follow rank-last or rank-first (C24), but the bank never lets the structural rule and the two parent cues disagree (64 of 64).
disputes.sides: R3-N3 (structural local rule) vs R6's node-local-cue concern, reduced to the two parent cues the bank cannot separate.
disputes.what_would_settle_it: Forward passes of the Helm final.pt files on counterfactual packets where the part has a second parent that the whole does not point to. Needs torch/GPU on Helm weights; owner-authorised work.

disputes.statement: Was the seed-20260919 last-checkpoint flip caused by the unwired F4 schedule (constant lr 0.003), or by start-point/last-step noise? The start-point side shows no rank-last pull (C25), and the flip moved away from the rank-last node (C11).

task.question: What are the trained values of round_rate (and round_mix) in the six Helm final checkpoints, i.e. how open is the reasoning loop after training?
task.how_to_test: Read-only, no torch import. For receipt_2026091{7,8,9}/checkpoints and receipt_helm1_certified_2026091{7,8,9}/checkpoints final.pt and initial.pt: open as a zip with zipfile, unpickle data.pkl with a custom pickle.Unpickler whose find_class stubs torch._utils._rebuild_tensor_v2 and torch storage classes, then read the raw little-endian float32 bytes of the round_rate (1 value) and round_mix entries from the archive's data/<key> members. Report g = 0.01 x tanh(round_rate) per run. PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, output to SCRATCH/RT3.
task.outcome_rules: Written before running. If unpickling needs anything beyond stubbing tensor/storage rebuilds -> UNREADABLE_WITHOUT_TORCH; stop, report, defer. If |g| < 0.001 in all six runs -> the loop is nearly shut after training; the design cap, not only the 1.0 wiring defect, keeps rounds weak (supports R7-N4). If |g| >= 0.005 in all three Helm 2.0 runs -> the loop is open; the ablation insensitivity means answers route around it (heads and input side-channels). Otherwise -> MIXED; report values. This is one factor only; the merge weights also scale the update, so no outcome alone proves the loop carries or lacks signal.

results.answer_plain:
I read the saved weights of all six Helm runs without torch. All files opened. I only had to stub the tensor and storage rebuild steps. The pickle also used Python's own OrderedDict, which is plain Python, not torch.

What g is. Helm has a reasoning loop of 8 rounds. Each round adds g times an update to every node's state. g = 0.01 x tanh(round_rate). round_rate starts at exactly 0.0 in all six runs, so g starts at 0. The size of g can never go above 0.01.

Trained g in the final checkpoints (seeds 20260917, 20260918, 20260919):
- Helm 1.0: -0.0016363888373763216, -0.002299261025249284, -0.0017775816018125582.
- Helm 2.0: 7.788207302131318e-05, 0.0025302752221345445, -2.5343871132809456e-06.

Result under the fixed rules: MIXED. Not all six are below 0.001. No Helm 2.0 run reaches 0.005.

What this means. This is inferred, not measured by a forward pass.
- In two of the three Helm 2.0 runs (seeds 20260917 and 20260919), the repaired loop ended almost shut. g also stayed below 0.0002 in size at all 14 saved checkpoints of those runs.
- For those two runs I used the stored weights to set an upper limit. One round can change a node's state by at most 0.0007784523332212379 and 1.920658204660671e-05 of its size.
- Only Helm 2.0 seed 20260918 opened its loop. That began between update 294 and update 441.
- All three Helm 1.0 loops were partly open. But in 1.0 every round got the same one-hop input, because of the known wiring defect.
- The tanh limit was never close. The largest |tanh(round_rate)| in the 84 checkpoint files I read was 0.2557200304034944, and the limit is 1. So training chose small values. The ceiling did not force them.
- Resetting the round group after training puts round_rate back to exactly 0. That shuts the loop fully. It moved held-back scores by -7/-2/-2 of 127 in 1.0 and -3/-6/+4 in 2.0. Resetting only the round's core block moved Helm 2.0 seeds 20260917 and 20260919 by 0.
- Loop openness does not line up with passing. Helm 2.0 seed 20260917 passed with a nearly shut loop. Seed 20260919 failed with a nearly shut loop. Seed 20260918 passed with the most open loop.

Limit. g is only one factor. To know whether the answers use the small loop signal, someone would need a forward pass. This task did not allow one.
results.outcome_under_rules: MIXED. Rule 1 (UNREADABLE_WITHOUT_TORCH) did not fire. find_class was asked for only four names in all 84 files read: torch._utils._rebuild_tensor_v2, torch.FloatStorage and torch.ByteStorage (all stubbed), plus collections.OrderedDict. OrderedDict comes from the Python standard library, not torch, and a plain pickle.Unpickler resolves it. I say this openly: if the chair reads 'anything beyond' to include standard-library classes, the rule-1 reading would change. Rule 2 (|g| < 0.001 in all six) FAILS. The three Helm 1.0 runs have |g| = 0.0016363888373763216, 0.002299261025249284 and 0.0017775816018125582, and Helm 2.0 seed 20260918 has |g| = 0.0025302752221345445. Rule 3 (|g| >= 0.005 in all three Helm 2.0 runs) FAILS. The largest Helm 2.0 |g| is 0.0025302752221345445, and the other two are 7.788207302131318e-05 and 2.5343871132809456e-06. So the 'Otherwise' branch applies: MIXED, values reported. As the rules say, g alone proves neither that the loop carries signal nor that it lacks it.

findings.claim: The tanh ceiling was never approached. Across all 84 files, the largest |tanh(round_rate)| was 0.2557200304034944 (Helm 2.0 seed 20260918, retained.pt), and the ceiling is 1. So the small g values are what training settled on. The 0.01 x tanh cap did not clip them. All runs used one AdamW group with lr 0.003, weight_decay 0.01 (decoupled), betas (0.9, 0.999) and eps 1e-08, for 1470 steps. round_rate still had non-zero gradient moments at the end. sqrt(bias-corrected exp_avg_sq) was 0.9541454382256298, 0.07723909238598554 and 0.048812157850729766 for 1.0, and 0.035481591668794624, 0.055358683268115626 and 0.019367985067276487 for 2.0. INFERRED: an AdamW step moves a parameter by roughly lr = 0.003 at most when the gradient sign holds steady. So 1470 updates could have moved round_rate by up to about 4.41, where tanh is close to 1. The optimizer did not do this. In Helm 2.0 seeds 20260917 and 20260919 the gradient on round_rate kept changing sign around 0. Whether the fixed 0.01 factor slows the opening of the loop is not isolated by any measurement.

findings.claim: This limit comes from stored weights only. It is not a forward pass. The core block has no bias: update = merge @ [tanh(left v), tanh(right v)] (pointer_learner.py:825-831). Every tanh output lies between -1 and 1. Hidden rows have RMS 1 (_rms_unit, :913-935). So one round changes a node's state by at most |g| x sqrt(mean_i L1(merge row i)^2), measured relative to the state's RMS. For the final checkpoints that limit is 0.03563534467346261, 0.04943479472968602 and 0.03358104069151053 (Helm 1.0, seeds 20260917/18/19), and 0.0007784523332212379, 0.05522824041609115 and 1.920658204660671e-05 (Helm 2.0). merge.weight Frobenius norm grew from about 4.6 at initial.pt to 17.579357427893193, 17.49552952386477 and 15.836339990739694 (1.0) and 8.446552902213345, 16.828943177656857 and 6.564389822069956 (2.0). The first number is rounded here; exact initial values are 4.622432080197718, 4.64177772211351 and 4.5839284355821865. INFERRED: over 8 rounds, Helm 2.0 seeds 20260917 and 20260919 can move a node's state by at most about 8 x 0.0007784523332212379 and 8 x 1.920658204660671e-05 of its size. So the states the heads read in those two runs are, within that limit, the one-shot encoding rms(node_encode(raw)). Such a small signal is unlikely to be a reliable multi-hop signal, though heads could in principle amplify small differences.

task.question: Does Helm's reach head choose its VIA node by the structural rule (common neighbour of whole and part) or by node-local cues? And do untrained models carry a built-in bias that makes each seed's gate result a start-point lottery?
task.how_to_test: Read-only pure JSON. For all six receipts, course_p00 and course_p10 predictions/scoring plus the six ablation_*_predictions.json, and world edges and declarations from records/typed_course_001/checks_002/public_course.json (public bank only; never sealed or private_targets files). For every reach record answered VIA, compare the chosen node with each cue: common neighbour (lexfirst), rank-last non-argument, rank-first non-argument, part's parent, node with both a parent and a child, highest declared participant rank. Report agreement overall and on records where the common-neighbour cue disagrees with each node-local cue. results.answer_plain:
Short answer: under the rules fixed before the run, the structural question comes out MIXED. The start-point question fits neither rule as I wrote it down, but there is no sign of a pull toward the rank-last node.

Terms used here:
- A "reach" question asks how one node (the part) is reached from another (the whole).
- The "VIA node" is the node Helm points at as the stop in between.
- The "common neighbour" is a node the whole points to and that points to the part.
- A "node-local cue" is a fact about one node on its own. Examples: its position in the sorted node list (its "rank"), its declared participant rank, or whether it has a parent.

Question 1: common neighbour or node-local cue? (all six final models, checkpoint p10)
- Helm answered VIA 440 times, over 74 different records.
- Where rank-last and the common neighbour point at different nodes, Helm picked the common neighbour 135 of 165 times.
- Where rank-first and the common neighbour differ, it picked the common neighbour 68 of 72 times.
- Where "highest participant rank" and the common neighbour differ, it picked the common neighbour only 14 of 30 times. This case covers just 5 records and 2 questions.
- So the fixed rule gives MIXED.

Why the result is MIXED:
- All of the disagreement comes from "diamond" worlds. In these, the whole-to-part path can go through either of two nodes.
- The checker picks the lower-ranked of the two.
- Helm cannot see rank, because the rank input was switched off in every run. The only input difference between the two nodes is the participant-rank flag.
- So on diamonds Helm has to break the tie with that flag. Which way it breaks the tie differs by seed.
- Where there is only one common neighbour, Helm follows it in 266 of 270 cases. The 4 misses are one question (36988555) in the Helm 2.0 seed 20260919 run.

A limit of the question bank:
- In every one of the 64 records that have a common neighbour, "a parent of the part" and "a node with both a parent and a child" pick the same node as the common neighbour.
- So this bank cannot tell the structural rule apart from those two node-local cues.

Question 2: do untrained models (checkpoint p00) have a built-in pull toward rank-last?
- No run points at the rank-last node at 2 times the chance rate or more. This holds in every version of the count.
- My main count gives ratios of 0.31 to 0.91. The ratio is observed rank-last pointers divided by the number expected by chance. It falls below chance in 4 runs because untrained models often point at the whole or the part themselves (240 of 577 times).
- If I count only pointers at other nodes, all six runs sit near chance (0.68 to 1.07).
- The frozen "floor" questions are the ones a no-learning rule already answers. The untrained starts got 2, 0, 2, 1, 0 and 0 of them right, and all were rank-last questions. That spread looks like ordinary chance, not a built-in rank pull.
- Question 36988555 was right at the start in 3 of 6 runs.

- There were 40 distinct disagreement records, which is 5 or more, so the result is not INCONCLUSIVE.
- Testable cues were rank-last, rank-first and highest participant rank.
- "Part's parent" and "node with both a parent and a child" were untestable: they have 0 disagreement records anywhere in the bank.
- Rank-last: common neighbour 135/165 = 0.8181818181818182; rank-last cue 30/165 = 0.18181818181818182.

- Per run (secondary): STRUCTURAL in Helm 2.0 seed 20260917 and Helm 1.0 seed 20260919. "SHORTCUT via highest participant rank" (4/5 = 0.8) in 2.0 seeds 20260918 and 20260919 and 1.0 seeds 20260917 and 20260918. That call rests on only 5 records and 2 questions.

START-POINT QUESTION: fits neither rule under my pre-set main count.
- The LOTTERY rule (2 times chance or more in at least 4 of 6 runs) is not met: 0 of 6 runs in all four count variants.
- The NO-BIAS rule was operationalized before running as a ratio between 2/3 and 3/2 in all six runs. The main count fails it: ratios are 0.589928, 0.393701, 0.906475, 0.735577, 0.305677 and 0.572988, and 4 runs fall below 2/3. The cause is untrained models pointing at argument nodes, which moves the ratio below chance, not above it.

results.answer_plain:
Short answer: the test the chair set cannot decide this. Under the fixed rule, the result is OPEN.

What I checked. Helm reads each node of a world as a row of numbers. It also reads a short "question" vector. I compared the values these inputs take in the four-node training worlds with their values on the ten-node panel. Nothing was run on a model. This was pure JSON reading.

Node rows: no new values. On the panel, every in-degree (number of parents), out-degree (number of children) and participant rank also occurs in training. The degree one-hot has slots for 0 to 4. Training and the panel both use in-degree 0-2 and out-degree 0-3. World count is 1 for every reach and parts question in both.

The question vector: new values. It carries the rank of the "whole" node as a plain number. (Rank = the node's position number in its world.) In training this number was only ever 0 to 3. On the panel it is 6 or 7 on all 59 questions.

Two more size-linked inputs to the reach answer head are also out of range on all 59 questions. These are the summed counts of root nodes and of leaf nodes.

Result under the rule. 63 of 63 misses are out of range. 21 of 21 hits are out of range. That is 100.0% against 100.0%, a gap of 0.0 points. Rule B applies: not explained by input range; OPEN.

Why that result is weak. Every question on the panel is out of range. So hits and misses were bound to have the same share. The panel contains no in-range questions to compare against.

What the other records show. This part is descriptive only, outside the rule. On four-node worlds, Helm answers DIRECT 5/5 on never-read worlds and 25/25 on trained worlds, in all six runs. On ten-node worlds it answers DIRECT 0 to 7 of 8. Every DIRECT miss said VIA instead. DIRECT and parts are one-step questions. Helm 2.0's loop repair did not help them. So these misses do not look like a reasoning-depth limit. They look like a change in world size that moves several inputs out of range at the same time. Which input causes the misses is still open. Settling it needs a forward run of the saved weights on relabelled worlds, and this round does not allow that.

new_open_questions: Which out-of-range input drives the ten-node DIRECT->VIA answers and the parts over-selection? Candidates: the raw whole-rank scalar in the query vector (6-7 vs 0-3), the two raw root/leaf degree sums in the reach head (59/59 out of range), node count in pooling and attention, or the novel node-row combinations. What would settle it: forward-only counterfactuals on saved final.pt, which need torch and are outside this round. (a) Relabel node indices so the whole argument lands at rank 0-3 with the graph unchanged. (b) Add disconnected distractor nodes to the five held-back four-node worlds, so size grows while argument ranks stay in range. (c) Replace the four reach-head degree terms with in-range values.

Should a size-transfer panel carry an in-range control, such as ten-node worlds whose whole argument has rank <= 3, or four-node worlds embedded in larger ones? Without one, the owner-set within-panel test cannot separate size from input range by pure JSON. This is an owner design decision.

task.question: Does any planned Helm 3.0 lab task (Q3-Q6) have answers that the project's own programs (checker, compiler, reference_ops) cannot compute from the model-visible input, and when does it enter the plan?

results.answer_plain:
Short answer: no. As the plan is written, every task from Q0 through Q6 has answers that the project's own programs compute exactly from what the model sees.

What I checked:
- Q3 data (families A, C, G, R). The "reference program" is the project's fixed code that makes the right answers: reference_ops.py for A and C, and the pinned CAS compiler for G and R. I ran it on every record the model is allowed to see in the train and dev files. It produced an answer for all 9,362 of them (A 2,469; C 2,304; G 2,304; R 2,285). Two runs gave identical answers.
- The A counts match the data's own manifest (642 and 100 admissible rows, 125 and 40 refusals). On 16 G dev records whose true answers sit in a run record, the compiler matched 16 of 16.
- The five operations that Q4 learned modules would copy. reference_ops.py reproduced all 61 of 61 contract cases from the inputs alone.
- The Helm difficulty ladder (the Q1 measuring set). My own short graph program reproduced all 1,072 of 1,072 answers from the world and the question.
- The plan documents: the answers for Q4 reconstruction come from the compiler. Q4 operations come from reference_ops. Q5 interventions use targets "independently computed" by the reference. Q6 keeps a verifier beside the learned answer. Every data record must carry a result from the reference program ("oracle").

Where "native interpretation" enters: nowhere in the current plan. In that task the model would read generated language and must produce the CAS expression. It is the only task type where the model's input is not what a project program reads. It has no task number among T00-T27 and no phase. It has no code and no data. The plan says "later". Its agreement record says to add it later as a separate experiment, and it is not needed for this release.

One caveat: T16 has not yet named the task families for the Q5 three-arm test. So this holds for the plan as written. Adding a new family would need a new decision.

Side finding: the ladder's rule for the VIA answer (which direct part the path to the target goes through) is not the frozen checker's rule. They give different answers on 18 of 373 VIA questions (5 of 373 under a different node-ordering assumption). The ladder's own file says it mirrors that rule.

What a future Q4 or Helm 3.0 pass could mean: the learned path copies the project's fixed programs and carries that over to new shapes and depths. It cannot show learning beyond those programs. The contracts file already says results mean "matches the code, never discovery".
results.outcome_under_rules: Rule 1 applies as written. Every task up to and including Q6 is reference-computable in the plan as written: TASKS.json and DIRECTIVE.md at HEAD 4eb98682, both unchanged since commit 64ddfbd1 (2026-09-21 05:47:59 -0700). This confirms C21 part (3): no planned task can show learning beyond the project's fixed programs before 'native interpretation, later' (DIRECTIVE.md:135). Native interpretation has no task id (T00-T27) and no phase. The plan puts it after the core release as 'a distinct experiment' (AGREEMENTS_AND_DIFFERENCES.md:43; DIRECTIVE.md:25). Stated limit, not a reinterpretation: T16 has not frozen its task families (templates/EXPERIMENT_PLAN.json:8 task_families []), so the confirmation covers the plan as written. A new family would need a new decision. This is advice for the owner; scheduling is his call.

task.question: Forward-only diagnostic of the saved Q4 checkpoint: does its output depend on its input, where does input information stop, and can it rebuild training-type rows?
task.how_to_test: GPU task 1 of 2, run first. Local RTX 4070, inference only, no training, results to SCRATCH/RT1 only, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1. Load records/q4_authorized_20260922/run_001/checkpoint (weights sha256 d54f57155a54cbd28621d92af9cb5f45e425c015a559cf80103966ccbf275477) with q4_checkpoint.load_checkpoint on cuda:0. (0) Sanity: re-decode the 16 dev inputs with free_decode and compare with run_001/dev_predictions.jsonl. (1) encode() the 16 dev inputs, the 128 seen rows (random.Random(20260921).shuffle(range(2048))[:128]; list SCRATCH/R5/used_rows.json) and 128 unseen train rows; report relative spread = mean pairwise L2 distance / mean vector norm. (2) For each dev input, next_logits after prefixes [BINARY] and [BINARY, PLUS] with true, zeroed and swapped (another input's) bottleneck; report logit[TIMES]-logit[PLUS] and logit[BINARY]-logit[STATE], and the fraction of inputs whose full greedy decode changes under swap/zero. (3) Free-decode the 128 seen and 128 unseen train rows; score canonical-exact by depth with the dict-equality checker (q4_smoke_job.py:388); count distinct outputs. (4) Teacher-forced mean cross-entropy on those rows and the 16 dev targets, beside the SCRATCH/R5 input-blind learners (online bigram, loss-weighted slot prior) on the same rows.
task.outcome_rules: Written before running. (a) If step 0 does not reproduce all 16 saved predictions exactly -> BUG in checkpoint save/load or decoding; stop and report. (b) If relative spread < 0.05 on dev and seen rows -> ENCODER COLLAPSE: the vector carries almost no input information. (c) If spread >= 0.05 but swap/zero changes the greedy decode on 0 of 16 inputs and every |logit gap change| < 0.1 -> DECODER IGNORES THE BOTTLENECK. (d) If swap/zero changes decodes on >= 2 of 16 or logit gaps shift by >= 0.5 -> input is used but too weakly to leave the prior. (e) If seen-row exact >= 1 at any depth -> the pipeline can map input to output; no gross BUG. (f) If seen and unseen train rows are 0 exact with 1-2 distinct outputs and teacher-forced CE on them is >= the input-blind CE on the same rows -> consistent with TOO LITTLE TRAINING; bug not excluded, go to RT2. Neither (b) nor (c) alone is a code defect; both are expected states of an under-trained strict bottleneck. None of these outcomes changes any claim status; results are scratch-only diagnostics.
task.settles: D2; part of D1 (bug vs not-yet-trained)

results.answer_plain:
Short answer: the saved Q4 model is not broken in how it is saved, loaded or decoded. It is barely using its input. The 0/16 result looks like a model that has not trained long enough. A bug is still not ruled out. Per rule (f), the next step is RT2.

What I did. I loaded the saved checkpoint on the local RTX 4070 and ran it forward only. There was no training. I read no sealed files and no eval files. Nothing was written into the repo. Every number below is DIAGNOSTIC_NOT_CLAIM_BEARING.

1. Sanity check. I decoded the 16 dev inputs again. All 16 match the saved predictions: same outcome, same tree, same step count. So saving, loading and decoding work.

2. The 64-number vector. The "bottleneck" is the 64 numbers the encoder hands to the decoder. It is almost the same for every input. "Relative spread" means how far apart the vectors are, compared with how long they are. It is 0.03772133314348652 on the 16 dev inputs. It is 0.06685149684077571 on the 128 rows the model trained on. Any two vectors point almost the same way: cosine 0.9911303112245342 or higher. In 55 of the 64 slots, the value is pinned near +1 or -1 whatever the input.

3. What the vector still carries. It does hold some facts about the END of the input. A plain class-average read-out gets "the root's right side is a sub-expression" right on 128 of 128 unseen rows. Always guessing the most common answer gets 60 of 128. It holds almost nothing about the START of the input: first-leaf noetic 9 of 128, against 8 of 128 for the most-common guess.

4. Does the decoder read the vector? Only its shared part. Replacing the vector with all zeros moves the decoder's choices by 0.64 to 0.71 logits. Swapping in another input's vector moves them by at most 0.013814. Neither change alters any of the 16 decoded trees. Even the all-zero vector decodes to the same tree, (^7^E + ^7^C).

5. How weak the input signal is. The decoder does respond to the right-side fact the vector carries, in the right direction. But the effect is 0.000460 logits, against a 1.1-logit margin. That is about 2,400 times too small to change the answer.

6. Rows it trained on. It rebuilt 0 of 128 training rows and 0 of 128 unseen training rows exactly, at every depth. All 256 got the same one tree.

7. Surprise scores. "Cross-entropy" measures how surprised the model is by the right answer (lower is better). I compared it with two simple count tables that never look at the input. On its own 128 training rows the model scores 1.621673. The count tables score 1.276293 and 1.154891. The model is worse on every one of those rows, and on every part of the answer, including the tree shape.

Rules as written: (a) no. (b) no: dev is below 0.05 but the trained rows are not, and I had fixed "both sets" before running. (c) no. (d) yes, but only because of the zeroed vector; the swapped vector moved gaps by less than 0.1. (e) no. (f) yes: go to RT2. No claim status changes.

findings.claim: Answer to dispute D2, the collapse locus: both parts are involved, and neither fully explains it. The encoder squeezes inputs into one saturated pattern. It keeps mainly end-of-input facts and loses the start (F2-F4). The decoder treats the vector's shared part as a fixed bias. It responds to the input-specific part by only 0.0005 to 0.005 logits, against 1.1 to 2.0 logit decision margins (F5, F6). The constant tree comes from the decoder's own weights: it appears even with an all-zero vector. On D1: no save/load/decode defect was found (F1). The model has not yet reached an input-blind level of fit even on its own training rows (F9). That fits under-training of a strict bottleneck. It does not prove more training would be enough: a left-to-right, final-state-only encoder that loses the start of the input may also limit what can be learned. No overfit test has been run, so a subtle bug is not excluded.

I ran RT2. It did not settle the question.

What I ran. I did one bounded re-training on the local RTX 4070. The model, seed, learning rate, clip and loss were the same as in today's smoke. It made 2,000 updates, cycling over 256 training rows, which is about 8 passes. Training took 28.9 seconds, so the 5-minute cap did not stop it. The model stayed in memory. Nothing was written into any repository. The rules were written down before the run (SCRATCH/RT2/PREREG_RT2.txt).

First check: my scratch driver copies the smoke faithfully. After 128 updates, its weights matched the smoke's saved weights bit for bit. All 128 losses matched the smoke's log.

Main result: after 2,000 updates the model got zero trees fully right. "Fully right" means the whole predicted expression tree equals the correct one. It scored zero on the 256 rows it trained on, zero on 128 other training rows with familiar tree shapes, and zero on all 256 dev rows. It also scored zero on the 105 simplest training rows, even though each row was trained 7 or 8 times. Not one row had its leaves right. The leaves are the single states at the tips of the tree, like ^7^E.

But the model was not stuck. The smoke's one repeated answer broke up between update 500 and update 1,000. By the end it gave 14 different answers on its training rows. It picked the right tree shape for 138 of those 256 rows. On training-type rows, its loss beat both input-blind references. An input-blind reference is a simple counter that never looks at the input.

On dev (tree shapes held out from training), it still did worse than the best input-blind counter. It never produced a dev shape. It always answered with a training shape or a tree that was too deep.

Reading against the rules fixed before the run: no rule fires.
- BUG needs 2 or fewer different answers. There were 14.
- TOO LITTLE TRAINING needs at least one fully right answer. There were none.
- DESIGN LIMIT needs 25% or more right at depth 3 on familiar shapes. The result was 0 of 38.
- SHAPE TRANSFER needs one right dev answer. The result was 0 of 256.

So the result fits none of the named outcomes.

My inference, not a rule result: the 128-update cap explains why the smoke gave one constant answer. It does not explain the zero score. With 15.6 times more updates, the model learns tree shape but not what goes in the leaves. D1 stays open. All numbers are DIAGNOSTIC_NOT_CLAIM_BEARING.
