results.answer_plain:
The grammar filter and the token codec have no bug on any visible row. The grammar filter (called the "mask") is the rule that decides which tokens the decoder may pick next. The codec is the code that turns a tree into tokens and back.

What I did. I read all 2,048 visible train rows and all 256 visible dev rows of family G. I used the project's own loader for this. For each row, R5's small parser turned the visible expression into a tree. Then ast_to_tokens turned that tree into the correct token list. Next I ran the real free_decode with a scripted scorer. At each step the scorer gave the correct token +100 and every other token 0. So the decoder can go wrong only if the mask refuses a correct token or the codec mangles something.

What happened. All 2,304 rows came back exactly right. On every row the decoder finished normally. The tokens matched, and the rebuilt tree was exactly equal to the parsed tree. The step count also equalled the token count. I made 51,288 separate step-by-step checks and the mask refused 0 correct tokens. At every leaf slot the mask allowed exactly the full set for that slot: 10 noetics, 5 domains, 8 drives or 6 registers. So the mask can neither block nor favour any leaf value.

Is the test able to catch a bug? Yes. I planted a fake bug in memory only: a mask that forbids the register token REG_T. The replay then failed on exactly the rows that contain a '|T' literal (709 train and 126 dev), and at exactly that slot.

The token table is consistent. It has 34 unique tokens, plus a separate start token numbered 34. The output head of the model scores len(TOKENS) = 34 outputs. The recorded parameter count of 70,818 can only be reached with 34 output tokens. All 7 runtime source files are byte-identical to the versions pinned for today's run, so I tested the same codec that ran. No torch was loaded at any point.

Limit. Correctness was judged against R5's parsed tree, not the sealed answer file, which I did not open. The parser matches the 16 saved reference trees exactly (16/16). Rendering each parsed tree back to text gives back the input exactly on 2,304/2,304 rows.

Under the rule fixed before the run, the mask and codec are cleared for every visible row. Any Q4 defect must be in the neural learning path.

task.question: Does the one Helm 2.0 run whose loop opened (seed 20260918, g 0.0025302752221345445) answer multi-hop reach better than the two runs whose loop stayed nearly shut (seeds 20260917 and 20260919)? This tests whether the open loop carries a signal the answers use.
task.how_to_test: Read-only pure JSON, no torch. For the six receipts, read course_p10_predictions.json and course_p10_scoring.json (trained and held-back reach) and development_p10_scoring.json (ten-node panel reach). Group reach records by the checker witness hop count (1, 2, 3, as RT4 did). Count correct per run and per hop group. task.outcome_rules: Written before running. If 2.0/20260918 is correct on at least 2 more 3-hop reach records (trained + held-back combined) than BOTH other 2.0 seeds AND at least 2 more than its own 1.0 run -> LOOP_SIGNAL_POSSIBLY_USED (one seed only, confounded with seed; not proof). If 2.0/20260918 is within +/-1 of both other 2.0 seeds on 2-hop and on 3-hop records -> NO_EVIDENCE_THAT_THE_OPEN_LOOP_IS_USED_FOR_MULTI_HOP. Otherwise -> MIXED; report numbers. Caveat fixed now: 3-hop VIA answers are one-hop relations to one marked node (RT4-F4), so even a positive result does not show multi-step propagation.

results.answer_plain:
Short answer: no. The saved answers show no multi-hop advantage for the one Helm 2.0 run whose loop opened (seed 20260918). Under the fixed rules the outcome is MIXED.

Terms used here:
- A "hop" is one link on the checker's path from the whole to the part. A 3-hop question has three links on that path.
- The "loop" is Helm's round-to-round update. Its size is set by g.
- A "diamond" is a record where two nodes tie as the answer. The checker breaks the tie by label order. Helm cannot see that label order (C24).

What I did:
- I rebuilt the frozen checker's path rule in plain Python and gave every reach record a hop count that does not depend on any run.
- The rebuild matches all 633 witnesses written in the files. It also reproduces all 960 correct/wrong marks.
- I counted correct answers per run and per hop group. The pure-Python scripts are in SCRATCH/RT9. No torch, no model, no GPU.

Main numbers (trained and held-back combined: 55 two-hop and 10 three-hop records):
- Helm 2.0 seed 20260917: 2-hop 48, 3-hop 9.
- Helm 2.0 seed 20260918 (open loop): 2-hop 50, 3-hop 10.
- Helm 2.0 seed 20260919: 2-hop 45, 3-hop 10.
- Helm 1.0 seeds 20260917 / 20260918 / 20260919: 2-hop 50 / 50 / 48, 3-hop 10 / 10 / 10.

On 3-hop records, the open-loop run is +1, +0 and +0 ahead of the other two 2.0 runs and its own 1.0 run. The first rule needs +2 against all three, so it does not fire. It could never have fired: seed 20260919 and the 1.0 run of seed 20260918 were already at 10 of 10.

On 2-hop records, the open-loop run is +2 and +5 ahead. The second rule needs every gap within 1, so it does not fire either. So the result is MIXED.

The 2-hop gaps come from two things that have nothing to do with the loop:
- Four records of one question (36988555), where seed 20260919 flipped at its last checkpoint.
- Diamond records, which each seed breaks its own way.

With the 16 diamond records removed, five runs score 38 of 39. Seed 20260919 scores 34 of 39.

The strongest fact: the open-loop run gives exactly the same answer as Helm 1.0 seeds 20260917 and 20260918 on all 107 course reach records. Helm 1.0's rounds only repeated one one-step update. My inference: nothing in these saved answers shows the open loop being used.

Two limits on the test:
- The bank barely tests multi-step reach. All 10 three-hop records have only one possible answer node, one link from a marked node. Only 2 of 55 two-hop records need path information, and all six runs get both right.
- The ten-node panel has 29 "no path" records that do need a reachability judgement. All six runs, the open-loop run included, get 0 of 29.

This is advice to the owner, not a claim-status change.
results.outcome_under_rules:
MIXED. The rules were fixed by the chair before the run. My operational reading was written to SCRATCH/RT9/00_PRE_RUN_DEFINITIONS.txt (sha256 995e6b6a4b3a96f6d76447e452a7917f1420fc61a7dfd5ad1b335dd4907e3547, 2026-09-23T02:38:26Z) before any count. It uses trained + held-back combined for both rules. Before writing it I had seen R3's pooled numbers (m1/m2/m3_out.txt) and C9, and I disclosed that in the file.

Rule 1 (LOOP_SIGNAL_POSSIBLY_USED) does not fire. 3-hop correct: H3(2.0/18) = 10, H3(2.0/17) = 9, H3(2.0/19) = 10, H3(1.0/18) = 10. The gaps are +1, +0, +0; the rule needs >= 2 on all three.

Rule 2 (NO_EVIDENCE_THAT_THE_OPEN_LOOP_IS_USED_FOR_MULTI_HOP) does not fire. The 3-hop gaps are within +/-1 (+1, +0). The 2-hop gaps are not: H2 = 50 vs 48 (+2) and 50 vs 45 (+5).

The outcome is therefore MIXED. The same MIXED holds under the secondary readings: adding the dev panel, adding excluded records, or held-back only. Only the dev-panel-only reading gives NO_EVIDENCE, and it is not the verdict.

I did not reinterpret the rules. One plain note: given the other runs' results, rule 1 was unreachable. 2.0/19 and 1.0/18 were already at the 10/10 ceiling on 3-hop, so the largest possible gap was +0.

task.question: Can the unchanged Q4 pipeline memorise 8 training rows exactly? And if not, does it fail on leaf content only, with the decoder ignoring row-specific bottleneck content? This separates BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs DESIGN LIMIT for D1.
task.how_to_test: The only GPU task this round (the one bounded diagnostic re-run). Local RTX 4070, at most 2,000 updates and at most 5 minutes wall time, results in SCRATCH/RT7 only, no commit, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, repo untouched. Reuse the RT2 scratch driver (SCRATCH/RT2/rt2_run.py, bit-faithful per RT2-F1) with one change: S8 = the first 8 rows of random.Random(20260921).shuffle(range(2048)) (the smoke's first 8 rows). Same StrictR1 width 64, seed 20260921, AdamW lr 0.001, clip 1.0, one example per update, same loss, cycling S8 for 2000 updates (250 passes). Targets from the R5 parser on visible observations (validated 2048/2048). Fidelity pre-check: the first 8 losses must equal updates 1-8 of run_001/updates.jsonl. Evaluate at 250, 500, 1000 and 2000 updates: (i) free-decode exact on S8 (dict equality, q4_smoke_job.py:388), with each row's depth; (ii) teacher-forced argmax token accuracy on S8 per slot class (expr, op, noetic, domain, drive, register, eos); (iii) teacher-forced CE on S8 per slot class with the TRUE bottleneck and with a SWAPPED bottleneck (row (i+1) mod 8's vector); (iv) bottleneck relative spread on S8 (RT1 definition); (v) mean training loss per 8-update pass. For context only (not a rule input): free-decode dev rows 1-16 at the end.
task.outcome_rules: Written before running. (0) If the fidelity pre-check fails -> SCRIPT_DEFECT; stop and report; no reading. If the 5-minute cap stops the run early -> BUDGET_LIMITED; apply the rules to the updates reached. Rules are read at the final evaluation. (A) FITS: S8 exact >= 7 of 8 -> no gross defect in the learning path; the pipeline can carry leaf content through the 64-number state for 8 rows; RT2's 0/256 is then a rate or capacity issue at 256 rows (TOO LITTLE TRAINING or capacity DESIGN LIMIT), not a BUG. (B) BUG_OR_OPTIMISATION_FAILURE: S8 exact <= 1 of 8 AND pooled leaf-slot (noetic+domain+drive+register) teacher-forced accuracy on S8 < 50% AND last-pass mean training loss > 0.5 -> a 70,818-parameter model cannot memorise 8 rows in 250 passes; recommend a code audit of the leaf path, not more training. (C) BOTTLENECK_NOT_USED: S8 exact <= 1 of 8 AND structure-slot (expr+op+eos) teacher-forced accuracy >= 95% AND pooled leaf-slot CE with SWAP minus CE with TRUE < 0.05 nats -> even under memorisation pressure the decoder learns shared structure but does not read row-specific content from the bottleneck; points to a DESIGN limit of the strict final-state bottleneck at this lr (or a defect in the bottleneck path), not to budget. If (B) and (C) both fire, report both; (C) is the more specific reading. (D) Otherwise (for example 2-6 of 8 exact) -> INCONCLUSIVE; report numbers only; D1 stays open. All results DIAGNOSTIC_NOT_CLAIM_BEARING; none changes any claim status.
task.settles: D1 (BUG vs TOO LITTLE TRAINING vs DESIGN LIMIT)

results.answer_plain:
Yes. The unchanged Q4 pipeline memorised all 8 training rows exactly. Rule A (FITS) fired.

What I ran: the RT2 scratch driver with one change. It trained only on the smoke's first 8 rows, over and over. That was 2,000 updates, or 250 passes. It ran on the local RTX 4070 and took 16.723 s. Nothing was written to the repository.

The copy check passed. It tests whether my copy of the training behaves exactly like the real run. The first 8 losses equal the smoke's first 8 losses exactly (8 of 8). The gradient sizes also match (8 of 8).

Results at the end (2,000 updates):
- 8 of 8 rows were rebuilt exactly. That includes all 4 depth-3 rows.
- In teacher-forced reading, the model is given the correct earlier tokens and must predict the next one. It got every slot type right 100% of the time.
- The mean training loss in the last pass was 0.008781951561104506.

The decoder does read row-specific content from the bottleneck. The bottleneck is the 64 numbers the encoder hands to the decoder. For the swap test, I gave each row another row's 64 numbers. The loss on leaf labels then rose from 0.013603749170075528 to 0.36831877462603957 nats. That is a rise of 0.35471502545596406, far above the 0.05 line.

How it got there matters. At 250 updates (about 31 showings of each row), the model still gave one fixed answer for all 8 rows. At that point, swapping the 64 numbers changed almost nothing (0.002352977887942309). That looks like the saved smoke checkpoint. By 1,000 updates, all 8 rows were right.

What this means under the rule written before the run:
- There is no gross bug in the learning path.
- The 64-number state can carry leaf content for 8 rows.
- So RT2's 0 of 256 is a speed or capacity issue at 256 rows, not a bug.

RT7 cannot tell speed from capacity. That part of D1 stays open.

Context only, not a rule input: on dev rows 1-16 the memorised model scored 0 of 16. It just repeats its 8 memorised trees. That is expected when a model memorises.

All numbers are DIAGNOSTIC_NOT_CLAIM_BEARING. They change no claim status.

dossier.why_helm_plain: Helm is the name of the learning part of the CNCM pointer machine. CNCM means CAS Native Cognitive Machine. Helm exists because the machine before it failed in a measured way. That machine learned the questions it practised, going from 13/18/17 to 84/85/86 of 189. It did not improve on worlds it had never practised, going from 2/3/3 to 5/3/2 of 45. A check that cost nothing showed the cause: its input blended all worlds into one vector, so a new world could not be read. On 2026-09-19 the owner chose a new design: read one world as a small graph, and answer by pointing at that world's own parts. Pointing makes the skill the same for every world. The owner's recorded purpose is learning inside the trained weights, "AT THE NEURON LEVEL", toward a working CASFORMER/CNCM, and gains from fixed rules do not count. The inputs carry no words. The test counts only the relational question kinds, because a shortcut that copies one flag had passed the older test. The records warned before the run that this test had low power. The name "Helm" first appears in commit 994950b5 on 2026-09-19. The record says only "The owner chose the name." No reason for the word is recorded anywhere the team searched, so only the owner can answer that.

why_not_pass_plain.helm_1_0: Helm 1.0 did pass the fixed grading program. MEASURED: it gained 10, 12 and 11 of the 18 frozen questions over its untrained start, with 0 losses, on all three seeds. READ: the grader compares each run with its own untrained start, not with a rule that learns nothing. MEASURED: a rule that learns nothing (the "floor") already answers 11 of the 18. Against that floor, Helm 1.0's net result is +1, +1 and 0. The only 2 questions it answered beyond the floor were the same 2 reach questions on every seed. Rules written after the results also answer those 2. A rule written before the run (LB18) answers the 5 analogy questions. MEASURED: Helm's analogy part gives one fixed world as the answer to all 70 analogy questions, so those 5 could never be won. MEASURED: a real wiring defect made its 8 reasoning rounds act as one round. INFERRED: no measurement shows that defect was the limit. INFERRED: the pass shows a climb from a random start up to the floor. It does not show learning beyond fixed rules.
why_not_pass_plain.helm_2_0: MEASURED: only one of three seeds failed. Seed 20260917 passed (11 gained, 1 lost, p = 13/4096). Seed 20260918 passed (12 gained, 0 lost, p = 1/4096). Seed 20260919 failed (7 gained, 1 lost, p = 9/256 = 0.03515625, above 1/100). The label NO_TRANSFER_TO_NEW_WORLDS is correct under the frozen rule. READ: BRAIN_LINEAGE.md wrongly says seed 20260917 failed, and wrongly says the gate needs zero losses. MEASURED: the failing seed's untrained start already had 4 of 18 right. It lost one reach question (36988555) only at the last checkpoint, and every earlier checkpoint passes. READ: the planned learning-rate decay (F4) was never switched on. MEASURED: on the 18 questions, Helm 2.0's final answers equal Helm 1.0's on two seeds and are one worse on the third. Leaving out correspondence, it is lower on held-back answers on every seed. Its one clear gain, correspondence 0 to 20 of 20, is matched by a rule that reads no links. MEASURED: the repaired loop ended nearly shut in 2 of 3 runs. The one run whose loop opened gives the same reach answers as two Helm 1.0 runs. INFERRED: the failure is fragile, and a pass would not have shown that 2.0 is better.
why_not_pass_plain.q4_smoke: READ: no accuracy target was set before the run, and the smoke was marked as not claim-bearing. So 0/16 is a negative observation, not a failed gate. READ: the Q4 model is a separate lab model, not Helm. MEASURED: it rebuilt 0 of 16 dev trees and gave one identical tree, (^7^E + ^7^C), for all 16. Its loss never got below simple counters that ignore the input. MEASURED: the dev rows use only tree shapes never seen in training, so anything that does not parse the input scores 0. MEASURED in follow-ups (diagnostics only, not claim-bearing): the checkpoint, the decoder and grammar filter, the token codec, and the training replay are all correct. MEASURED: on 8 training rows, the unchanged pipeline memorised all 8 exactly. MEASURED: after 2,000 updates on 256 rows it still rebuilt 0 trees, although it learned tree shape. INFERRED: a code bug is excluded at the level tested. OPEN: whether the rest is too little training or a size limit of the 64-number hand-off.
why_not_pass_plain.common_root: INFERRED from measured parts. First, results were read against weak references. The untrained start was used instead of the no-learning floor, and the cheapest baselines were registered instead of the strongest. Stronger references had been written down before the runs, but they never reached the pass rule. Second, one kind of defect keeps coming back: a part exists but nothing reads it or feeds it. Examples are Helm 1.0's unused loop variable, the unwired learning-rate decay, the analogy scorer that never sees the focus world, and the rescorer that never compares per-seed passes. Tests checked the wiring, not the effect. Third, MEASURED: every task built or planned up to Q6 has an exact answer that the project's own fixed programs compute from the model's visible input. So a pass could only show imitation plus transfer. Fourth, the course bank barely tests multi-step reasoning. Fifth, many agents working on shared branches, killed runs and in-place edits cost evidence.

judgment.why_helm_answer_plain:
What Helm is (READ-FROM-RECORD). Helm is the name of the learning part of the CNCM pointer machine. CNCM means CAS Native Cognitive Machine. The learning part is the neural network whose numbers change in training. Helm 1.0 is the last certified version. Helm 2.0 is an experiment. Helm 3.0 is only planned. It has not been built.

Why it was built (READ-FROM-RECORD). The machine before Helm learned the questions it practised. Its score on them rose from 13, 18 and 17 to 84, 85 and 86 of 189. A "world" here is a small made-up machine with named parts and links. On five worlds it never practised, it stayed flat. Its scores there went from 2, 3 and 3 to 5, 3 and 2 of 45. A check that cost nothing found the cause. Every question's input mixed all 64 worlds into one 64-number blend. So a world it had not practised could not be read. Sources: records/typed_practice_001/PRACTICE_STUDY_RESULT.md:26-27 and records/HANDOFF_20260919_CNCM_POINTER_MACHINE.md:16-24.

The fix (READ-FROM-RECORD). On 2026-09-19 the owner chose "pointer answers plus the checkpoint check". A pointer answer says "this part here", inside the world being read. That skill works the same way in any world. Agents then told him that pointing alone would not work. The input also had to change, so that the machine reads one world as a small graph. His ruling: gains from hand-written rules never count as machine progress (HANDOFF_20260919_CNCM_POINTER_MACHINE.md:93-96).

why_not_pass_answer_plain.helm_1_0:
Short answer: Helm 1.0 did pass its grading program. The pass shows less than it seems.

MEASURED. Out of 18 fixed test questions, it gained 10, 12 and 11 over its untrained start, with 0 losses. The chance of that by luck was 1/1024, 1/4096 and 1/2048. The bar was 1/100.

READ-FROM-RECORD. The grading program compares each run with its own untrained start. It prints the score of a rule that learns nothing beside the result, but does not subtract it. That was a written design choice.

MEASURED. A rule that learns nothing already gets 11 of the 18. Helm 1.0 ended at 12, 12 and 11. That is +1, +1 and 0 above the rule.

MEASURED. Its only answers beyond the rule were the same two reach questions in every run. A reach question asks whether one part can be reached from another, and through which part. It also missed one question the rule gets right (404166e8), in every run.

MEASURED. Its analogy part gave the same world for all 70 analogy records. So it could never win the 5 analogy questions.

MEASURED. Almost all of the gain came in the first of ten training passes. After pass 1 the score was 11, 12 and 11. Then it stayed flat.

READ-FROM-RECORD. A wiring bug made its 8 reasoning rounds act as one round.

INFERRED. No measurement shows that this bug set the limit.

INFERRED. The neurons did learn something. From a random start they learned to answer like the simple rules, on worlds they had not seen. The design counted that as the skill. It does not show learning beyond those rules.
why_not_pass_answer_plain.helm_2_0:
Short answer: one of three runs fell short. The repairs did not make learning keep climbing.

MEASURED. The grading program printed NO_TRANSFER_TO_NEW_WORLDS.
- Run 20260917 passed: 11 gained, 1 lost. Luck chance 13/4096.
- Run 20260918 passed: 12 gained, 0 lost. Luck chance 1/4096.
- Run 20260919 failed: 7 gained, 1 lost. Luck chance 9/256 = 0.03515625, which is above the 1/100 bar.
With one loss, a run needs 10 gains.

MEASURED. The failing run's untrained start already had 4 of 18 right. That left fewer questions it could gain. It lost question 36988555 only at the very last checkpoint. At every earlier checkpoint it would have passed.

READ-FROM-RECORD. The planned slow-down of the learning rate (F4) was never switched on.

MEASURED. Helm 2.0 was meant to make the learning curve keep climbing. It did not. All three runs reached 11 or 12 of 18 after the first pass. Then they stayed flat or wobbled, ending at 12, 12 and 10.

MEASURED. On the 18 questions, its final answers equal Helm 1.0's in two runs and are one worse in the third.

MEASURED. Its repaired loop ended nearly shut in 2 of 3 runs. In the one run where the loop opened, it answered all 107 practice reach records exactly like two Helm 1.0 runs.

MEASURED. Its one clear gain was correspondence: matching parts one-to-one between two worlds. It went from 0 to 20 of 20. A rule that reads no links gets the same result. Correspondence was also outside the pass test.

READ-FROM-RECORD. The lineage file is wrong on two points. It says run 20260917 failed. It says the test needs zero losses (BRAIN_LINEAGE.md:231, :234-235).

INFERRED. The failure is fragile. It turned on one lucky start and one last flip. A pass would not have shown that 2.0 is better than 1.0.

OPEN. Why the loop did not matter: the loop's small step limit, or a question bank that barely needs multi-step answers.
why_not_pass_answer_plain.q4_smoke:
Short answer: it was an engineering test with no pass mark, and it rebuilt nothing.

READ-FROM-RECORD. No accuracy target was set before the run. The plan has no accuracy field. The job writes fixed labels that say the result is not certified. The directive says this kind of smoke test cannot support a capability claim.

READ-FROM-RECORD. The Q4 model is not Helm. It is a separate lab model. It is a small GRU, a simple step-by-step neural network. It reads the expression text, squeezes it into 64 numbers, then writes a tree back out.

MEASURED. It rebuilt 0 of 16 development trees. It gave the same tree for all 16: (^7^E + ^7^C).

MEASURED. Its training loss was still falling at the end. It was still worse than the best simple counters that ignore the input.

MEASURED. All 16 trees had shapes never seen in training.

INFERRED. So a method that does not truly read the input cannot score here.

READ-FROM-RECORD. The 128-update limit came from the directive's smoke-test template. It was part of the job shown to the owner before he authorized runs.

MEASURED by the team (diagnostic only):
- No code bug was found where they checked.
- The same code memorised 8 training rows exactly.
- After 2,000 updates on 256 rows it still rebuilt 0 trees.

OPEN. What limits it now. It may need more training. The 64-number hand-off may be too small. The way the hand-off carries the input may be the problem. Or it may be how training behaves.
why_not_pass_answer_plain.common_root:
INFERRED from measured parts.

First, the yardstick was weak. Each run was compared with its own random start, not with rules that learn nothing. That was a written choice. It let a climb up to the no-learning level count as a pass.

Second, simple fixed programs could answer the tests. The project's own programs compute every answer from what the machine sees. The 'new' worlds reuse practised shapes. So even a pass could only show a simple rule copied onto relabelled worlds.

Third, parts were built but never fed or never read. Examples:
- the unused loop variable in Helm 1.0;
- the learning-rate slow-down that was never wired in;
- the analogy part that never sees the world it is asked about;
- the checking tool that never compares each run's pass.
The tests checked the wiring, not the effect.

Fourth, the pass test was known to be weak before the runs.

Fifth, the process lost evidence and copied rules wrongly. A killed run left Helm 0.1 impossible to certify. A reworded 'zero losses' rule spread into several records.

READ-FROM-RECORD. The owner chose 'Stratify AND train longer'. Training still stayed at ten passes (docs/CNCM_TYPED_POINTER_STUDY_v0.1.md:94-95; pointer_contract.py:90). I found no owner decision for that.

MEASURED. In all six Helm runs, almost all learning happened in the first pass.

INFERRED. The machines latched onto a simple rule early and then stopped improving.

judgment.plain_english_verdict: Helm is the learning network inside the CNCM pointer machine. It was built because the earlier machine could not read worlds it had never practised. The owner chose the pointing fix, then accepted that the input had to change too. Why he named it "Helm" is not written down, so only he can say. Helm 1.0 passed its grading program, but that program compared it only with its own random start. A rule that learns nothing already scores 11 of 18, and Helm 1.0 scored 12, 12 and 11. So the 1.0 pass shows learning up to the level of simple rules, not beyond them. Helm 2.0 failed because one of its three runs gained 7 and lost 1, which misses the 1-in-100 luck bar. Its repairs did not make learning keep climbing: every run was flat after the first pass. Today's Q4 run is a separate lab model with no pass mark, and it rebuilt 0 of 16 trees. No code bug was found in Q4, and whether it needs more training or a different design is still open. The shared root is a weak yardstick plus tests that simple fixed programs already solve. Several records misstate the pass rule or the results and should get dated corrections. These rulings are advice only, and claim status still comes from the fixed programs and the owner.
